subject: Culture
title: Mourning Colors
description: A quick, practical guide to Mourning Colors.

hook.text: In the West, mourners wear black. In East Asia, white is the color of death.

buildup.text: Black became Europe's mourning color in the Roman Empire. It signaled withdrawal from public life.

discovery.text: In India, white marks mourning because it's the absence of color—stripped of worldly joy.

twist.text: In parts of Africa, red is the mourning color. It represents the blood of the lost.

climax.text: No culture mourns without color. But the palette of grief changes with every border.

punchline.text: Grief is universal. Its wardrobe is not.

quiz.question: In traditional Indian mourning, what color is typically worn?

details.summary: The color of grief varies around the world. Western cultures wear black for mourning, but in much of East Asia white is the death color. Hindu mourners wear white. In parts of Africa, red symbolizes mourning. Egypt uses yellow. The color of sorrow is entirely culturally determined.
details.whyItMatters: Mourning color differences catch travelers and expatriates off guard. Wearing the wrong color to a funeral in another culture can cause serious offense during an already emotional occasion.
takeaways: Black is the mourning color in most Western cultures
White is the color of death in China, India, and much of Asia
Some African cultures use red to symbolize mourning

faq.question: Why does the West use black for mourning?
faq.answer: Black has represented mourning in the West since the Roman Empire, where dark togas signaled grief. Queen Victoria's extended mourning after Prince Albert's death in 1861 cemented black as the standard.

faq.question: Why is white the mourning color in Asia?
faq.answer: In Chinese philosophy, white represents purity and is associated with death and the afterlife. White mourning clothes signify respect and a clean passage for the deceased. In Hinduism, white represents detachment from worldly pleasures, appropriate for mourning.
